title: Commercial crops are no forest right, Supreme Court says; ex-CJI Gavai to head Megamalai panel
dek: The court was ruling on claims by about 4,600 people farming silk cotton on 5,000 hectares inside a Tamil Nadu tiger reserve.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Growing a commercial crop on forest land does not by itself give anyone a right to stay there under the Forest Rights Act, the Supreme Court has ruled, in a case over thousands of people farming silk cotton inside a tiger reserve in Tamil Nadu. The court has set up a special committee headed by former Chief Justice of India B.R. Gavai to scrutinise the claims.

"The cultivation of a commercial crop cannot, therefore, be recognised as a forest right," a bench of Justice Vikram Nath and Justice Sandeep Mehta said in its judgment on Friday in A. John Kennedy and others v. State of Tamil Nadu and others. The case concerns the Megamalai forests, part of the Srivilliputhur-Megamalai Tiger Reserve in the Western Ghats.

## What the court found

According to the state's figures, as recorded in reports of the judgment, 4,594 people occupy 5,072.64 hectares of forest land in the area, and 3,637.83 hectares of that is under silk cotton. The occupants fall into three groups: 1,595 who live and farm inside the forest, 232 who farm there with only temporary shelter, and 2,767 who live outside the forest boundary but farm inside it.

The Forest Rights Act of 2006 recognises the rights of Scheduled Tribes and other traditional forest dwellers to land they have lived on and cultivated, and to collect minor forest produce. Tamil Nadu argued that silk cotton was traditional minor forest produce that the government had encouraged. The court disagreed, finding no material recognising it as minor forest produce under the Act. "The concept of planned cultivation of commercial crop is totally contrary to the very concept" of the Act, it said, according to reports of the judgment.

The bench held that people in the second and third groups could not qualify as forest dwellers simply because they farm forest land. Those claiming as "other traditional forest dwellers" must show three generations, or 75 years, of occupation before 13 December 2005, as the Act requires; present occupation alone is not enough. The court also criticised the Tamil Nadu government for delays in handling claims under the Act.

## The directions

The court constituted a special committee headed by Justice Gavai, who retired as Chief Justice in November 2025. Its other members are an officer of the Central Empowered Committee, the court's expert body on forest matters, and Tamil Nadu's Principal Chief Conservator of Forests. The committee will examine the orders passed on claims under the Act and report to the court in a sealed cover.

Tamil Nadu must set up the remaining gram sabhas, the village assemblies that first examine forest-rights claims, within 30 days, and decide the claims within five months after that. It must file monthly progress reports. About 40 gram sabhas have been set up so far and about 1,600 claims received, according to the state's figures as reported.

The Central Empowered Committee has been asked for its opinion on whether silk cotton can be treated as minor forest produce at all. The case was heard alongside the long-running T.N. Godavarman forest case, under which the Supreme Court has supervised forest protection across India since 1995.

## Why it matters

Tiger reserves across India contain farmland, settlements and claims under the Forest Rights Act, and courts and governments have struggled to balance the rights of forest-dwelling communities with wildlife protection. The ruling draws a line between subsistence use protected by the Act and commercial plantations, and is likely to be cited in disputes over encroachment in other protected areas. Forest-rights groups have long warned that strict readings of the Act can lead to evictions of genuine claimants; the court's order leaves individual claims to be decided through the gram sabha process.

## What happens next

The state's first status report is due when the case is next listed, on 1 February 2027.
